title: Dividing with a Remainder
description: What the lemma says and why the remainder is always smaller than the divisor.

blocks.heading: The idea
blocks.body: Divide 17 by 5: you get 3 groups of 5 and 2 left over. So 17 = 5 x 3 + 2. The leftover is always less than 5, otherwise you could make another group.

blocks.heading: The lemma
blocks.body: a = bq + r, where 0 <= r < b

blocks.heading: Remember
blocks.body:
q and r are unique
r can be 0
b must be positive

blocks.heading: Try it
blocks.body: Write 58 in the form 7q + r. 58 = 7 x 8 + 2, so q = 8, r = 2.

title: Euclid's Algorithm for HCF
description: Repeat the lemma until the remainder is zero to find the HCF fast.

blocks.heading: Why it works
blocks.body: Any common factor of a and b also divides r = a - bq. So HCF(a, b) = HCF(b, r), and the pair keeps getting smaller.

blocks.heading: Worked example
blocks.body: HCF(196, 38220): 38220 = 196 x 195 + 0. Remainder is already 0, so HCF = 196.

blocks.heading: Checklist
blocks.body:
Larger number first
Stop at remainder 0
Answer is the last divisor, not the last quotient

title: Prime Factorisation
description: Break numbers into primes using a factor tree and see why the result is unique.

blocks.heading: Building blocks
blocks.body: Primes are the atoms of numbers. 360 = 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 x 3 x 5 = 2^3 x 3^2 x 5, and no other list of primes multiplies to 360.

blocks.heading: Method
blocks.body:
Divide by the smallest prime repeatedly
Move to the next prime when it stops dividing
Write the answer with exponents

blocks.heading: Example
blocks.body: Factorise 1001: 1001 = 7 x 11 x 13.

title: HCF and LCM from Primes
description: Use prime factorisations to get HCF and LCM and check with the product rule.

blocks.heading: Rules
blocks.body:
HCF: smallest power of each common prime
LCM: largest power of every prime present
HCF x LCM = a x b

blocks.heading: Why 3^n never ends in 0
blocks.body: A number ending in 0 needs both 2 and 5 as prime factors. 3^n has only 3s, so it never ends in 0.

blocks.heading: Traps
blocks.body:
HCF uses the smallest powers
The product rule is for two numbers only

title: Zeros of a Polynomial
description: What a zero means algebraically and on the graph.

blocks.heading: Definition
blocks.body: k is a zero of p(x) if p(k) = 0. For p(x) = x^2 - 4, both 2 and -2 are zeros because they make p(x) zero.

blocks.heading: On the graph
blocks.body: The curve of a quadratic is a parabola. Its zeros are where it cuts the x-axis. It can cut twice, touch once, or never meet the axis.

blocks.heading: Check
blocks.body: Is 3 a zero of x^2 - 2x - 3? p(3) = 9 - 6 - 3 = 0. Yes.

title: Sum and Product of Zeros
description: The relations between zeros and coefficients, and how to build a polynomial from its zeros.

blocks.heading: Relations
blocks.body: For ax^2 + bx + c: alpha + beta = -b/a and alpha x beta = c/a

blocks.heading: Verify
blocks.body: 3x^2 - 12x + 9: zeros 1 and 3. Sum 4 = 12/3, product 3 = 9/3.

blocks.heading: Build
blocks.body: Zeros 2 and -5: sum -3, product -10. Polynomial x^2 + 3x - 10.

blocks.heading: Watch out
blocks.body:
The minus sign in -b/a
a is the coefficient of x^2, not of x

title: Recognising a Quadratic
description: Rearrange any equation into ax^2 + bx + c = 0 and read the coefficients.

blocks.heading: Standard form
blocks.body: A quadratic equation has degree 2 once simplified. Expand brackets, move everything to one side, and combine like terms before deciding.

blocks.heading: Example
blocks.body: (x - 2)(x + 1) = x^2 - 3 becomes x^2 - x - 2 = x^2 - 3, so -x + 1 = 0. The square terms cancel: not a quadratic.

blocks.heading: Rule
blocks.body:
a is never 0 in a quadratic
Read b and c only from the standard form

title: Forming Quadratics from Word Problems
description: Turn a story into an equation by choosing the unknown well.

blocks.heading: Method
blocks.body: Let the unknown be the quantity asked for. Translate each sentence into an expression. Set up the equality the problem describes. Rearrange to standard form.

blocks.heading: Example
blocks.body: The product of two consecutive positive integers is 306. Let the smaller be x: x(x + 1) = 306, so x^2 + x - 306 = 0.

blocks.heading: Example
blocks.body: A train covers 480 km at speed x km/h. If it were 8 km/h slower it would take 3 h more: 480/(x - 8) - 480/x = 3, which simplifies to x^2 - 8x - 1280 = 0.

title: Splitting the Middle Term
description: The core factorisation technique, step by step.

blocks.heading: The technique
blocks.body: For ax^2 + bx + c, find two numbers whose product is a x c and whose sum is b. Rewrite bx as the sum of those two terms, then factor by grouping.

blocks.heading: Example with a = 1
blocks.body: x^2 + 5x + 6: product 6, sum 5 gives 2 and 3. (x + 2)(x + 3) = 0, so x = -2 or -3.

blocks.heading: Signs
blocks.body:
Product positive, sum positive: both positive
Product positive, sum negative: both negative
Product negative: one of each, larger magnitude takes the sign of b

title: The Quadratic Formula
description: Solve any quadratic with the formula and know when to reach for it.

blocks.heading: Formula
blocks.body: x = [-b +/- sqrt(b^2 - 4ac)] / 2a

blocks.heading: When to use it
blocks.body: Use the formula when the middle term will not split neatly, or when the roots are irrational. It always works when b^2 - 4ac >= 0.

blocks.heading: Common slips
blocks.body:
Write -b, then square b separately
Divide the whole numerator by 2a
Simplify the square root before dividing

title: Word Problems and Checking Roots
description: Set up, solve, then reject roots that make no sense.

blocks.heading: Reject impossible roots
blocks.body: Lengths, ages, counts and speeds cannot be negative or fractional when the story says they are whole. Always check both roots against the situation.

blocks.heading: Example
blocks.body: A rectangle has area 60 and its length is 7 more than its breadth. b(b + 7) = 60 gives b^2 + 7b - 60 = 0, (b + 12)(b - 5) = 0. b = -12 is rejected; breadth 5, length 12.

blocks.heading: Example
blocks.body: Two numbers differ by 3 and their product is 54: x(x + 3) = 54, x^2 + 3x - 54 = 0, (x + 9)(x - 6) = 0, so 6 and 9, or -9 and -6 if negatives are allowed.

blocks.heading: Always
blocks.body:
Substitute each root back into the original equation
Answer the question asked, not just x

title: The Discriminant
description: Predict the type of roots without solving.

blocks.heading: Discriminant
blocks.body: D = b^2 - 4ac

blocks.heading: Three cases
blocks.body:
D > 0: two distinct real roots
D = 0: two equal real roots
D < 0: no real roots

blocks.heading: Example
blocks.body: x^2 + x + 1 = 0: D = 1 - 4 = -3, no real roots.

title: Finding Unknown Coefficients
description: Use D = 0 to find a parameter that gives equal roots.

blocks.heading: Method
blocks.body: Write D in terms of the unknown, set it equal to 0, solve the resulting equation. Check that a is still non-zero.

blocks.heading: Example
blocks.body: 2x^2 + kx + 3 = 0 has equal roots: k^2 - 24 = 0, so k = +/- 2 sqrt 6.

blocks.heading: Example
blocks.body: kx(x - 2) + 6 = 0 has equal roots: kx^2 - 2kx + 6 = 0, D = 4k^2 - 24k = 0, so k = 6 (k = 0 rejected).

title: Velocity and Time
description: The first equation of motion and the meaning of acceleration.

blocks.heading: Acceleration
blocks.body: Acceleration is the change in velocity per second. If a car goes from 10 m/s to 20 m/s in 5 s, its velocity changed by 10 m/s over 5 s, so a = 2 m/s^2.

blocks.heading: First equation
blocks.body: v = u + at

blocks.heading: Units
blocks.body:
Velocity in m/s
Acceleration in m/s^2
Time in s
Convert km/h by multiplying by 5/18

title: Displacement Equations
description: The second and third equations and how to choose between them.

blocks.heading: Choosing
blocks.body: List what you know and what you want. If time is not involved, use v^2 = u^2 + 2as. If final velocity is not involved, use s = ut + (1/2)at^2.

blocks.heading: Example
blocks.body: A ball dropped from rest falls for 3 s (a = 10 m/s^2): s = 0 + 0.5 x 10 x 9 = 45 m.

blocks.heading: Example
blocks.body: A bike at 15 m/s brakes at -3 m/s^2 to rest: 0 = 225 + 2(-3)s, so s = 37.5 m.

blocks.heading: Signs
blocks.body:
Choose the direction of motion as positive
Retardation gives negative a

title: Writing and Balancing Equations
description: From word equation to balanced symbol equation with states.

blocks.heading: Why balance
blocks.body: Atoms rearrange in a reaction but none appear or vanish. A balanced equation shows this with equal atom counts on both sides.

blocks.heading: Steps
blocks.body:
Write correct formulas
Count atoms of each element
Adjust coefficients, starting with the element in the fewest formulas
Balance H and O last
Recheck everything

blocks.heading: Example
blocks.body: Zn + HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2. Cl: 1 vs 2, so 2HCl. Now H: 2 vs 2. Balanced: Zn + 2HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2.

blocks.heading: Example
blocks.body: C3H8 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O. C: 3CO2. H: 4H2O. O on right: 6 + 4 = 10, so 5O2. Balanced: C3H8 + 5O2 -> 3CO2 + 4H2O.

title: Types of Reactions
description: Combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement and redox with everyday examples.

blocks.heading: Combination and decomposition
blocks.body: Combination: two substances form one (CaO + H2O -> Ca(OH)2). Decomposition: one breaks into several, often by heat, light or electricity (2H2O -> 2H2 + O2 by electrolysis).

blocks.heading: Displacement
blocks.body: A more reactive element pushes out a less reactive one: Fe + CuSO4 -> FeSO4 + Cu. The blue solution turns green.

blocks.heading: Double displacement and redox
blocks.body: Ions swap partners: Na2SO4 + BaCl2 -> BaSO4 + 2NaCl (white precipitate). In redox one substance gains oxygen (oxidised) while another loses it (reduced).

blocks.heading: Spotting them
blocks.body:
Two in, one out: combination
One in, many out: decomposition
Element swaps with element: displacement
Ions swap: double displacement

title: Module 1: Laws of Reflection and Spherical Mirrors
description: Understand converging concave and diverging convex mirrors, focal point, and ray tracing rules.

blocks.heading: Core Principle
blocks.body: When light rays hit a smooth curved mirror surface, each individual ray strictly obeys the law of reflection (i = r). A concave mirror curves inwards like a cave, focusing parallel incident rays into a real focal point in front of it. A convex mirror curves outwards, causing parallel rays to diverge as if originating from a focal point behind the mirror.

blocks.heading: Ray Tracing Rules
blocks.body:
1. A ray parallel to the principal axis passes through (or appears to diverge from) the principal focus after reflection.
2. A ray passing through the center of curvature retraces its path back along the same normal line.
3. A ray directed towards the pole reflects symmetrically at the same angle to the principal axis.

blocks.heading: Fundamental Relationship
blocks.body:
f = R / 2
For concave mirror: f < 0, R < 0
For convex mirror: f > 0, R > 0

title: Module 2: Mirror Formula & Numerical Problem Solving
description: Master Cartesian coordinate sign conventions, image calculations, and magnification.

blocks.heading: Cartesian Sign Convention
blocks.body: Always take the Pole (P) as the origin (0,0). All distances measured in the direction of incident light (to the right) are taken as positive (+), while distances measured against incident light (to the left) are negative (-). The heights measured upward normal to the principal axis are positive (+), and downward are negative (-).

blocks.heading: Class 10 Board Example
blocks.body: An object 4 cm in size is placed at 25 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. Find image distance: 1/v = 1/(-15) - 1/(-25) = -1/15 + 1/25 = -2/75 => v = -37.5 cm. Height h' = -(-37.5/-25)*4 = -6 cm (real, inverted, magnified).

title: Module 1: Snell's Law & Refractive Index
description: How light bends across optical boundaries, absolute and relative refractive indices.

blocks.heading: Mechanism of Refraction
blocks.body: Light slows down when passing from an optically rarer medium (like air) into an optically denser medium (like water or glass). To minimize travel time (Fermat's principle), the wave front changes direction, bending toward the normal. When speeding up from denser to rarer, it bends away from the normal.

blocks.heading: Snell's Mathematical Law
blocks.body:
n1 * sin(i) = n2 * sin(r)
Refractive index of glass ~ 1.5, water ~ 1.33, diamond ~ 2.42

title: Module 2: Lens Formula & Dioptres Power
description: Calculate real and virtual images for convex/concave lenses and combination optical power.

blocks.heading: Lens Characteristics
blocks.body: A convex lens is thicker at the center and thinner at the edges. It converges incident parallel rays to a real focus on the opposite side (f > 0). A concave lens is thinner at the center and diverges rays, yielding a virtual focal point (f < 0).

blocks.heading: Lenses Master Formulae
blocks.body:
1/f = 1/v - 1/u
m = v/u
P = 1/f(m)
P_net = P1 + P2

title: Module 1: Optical Anatomy & Accommodation
description: Structure of the eye: Cornea, Iris, Pupil, Crystalline Lens, Retina, and Ciliary Muscles.

blocks.heading: How We See
blocks.body: Light enters the eye through the cornea, passes through the pupil whose diameter is actively regulated by the muscular iris. The flexible crystalline lens forms a real inverted image onto the retina, which sends electrical impulses to the brain via the optic nerve.

blocks.heading: Key Anatomy Checklist
blocks.body:
• Cornea: Primary refraction boundary
• Iris: Colored diaphragm adjusting light ingress
• Ciliary muscles: Change lens curvature for focal accommodation
• Retina: Photoreceptor screen (Rods & Cones)

title: Module 2: Defects of Vision & Lens Corrections
description: Myopia, Hypermetropia, Astigmatism, Presbyopia, and corrective ray diagrams.

blocks.heading: Defects and Remedies
blocks.body: When the eyeball is too long, rays from distant objects converge before reaching the retina: Myopia, solved by a diverging concave lens. When the eyeball is too short, near rays converge behind the retina: Hypermetropia, solved by a converging convex lens.

title: Module 1: Glass Prism & Rainbow Formation
description: Prism deviation, angular dispersion, and rain drop internal reflection.

blocks.heading: Newton's Experiment
blocks.body: Isaac Newton first used a glass prism to split sunlight into a spectrum. Placing an inverted second prism in front of the spectrum recombined all colors back into white light, proving white light is composed of 7 spectral colors.

title: Module 2: Atmospheric Wonders & Scattering
description: Twinkling stars, atmospheric delay, blue skies, and crimson sunsets.

blocks.heading: Scattering Physics
blocks.body: Molecules of N2 and O2 in the upper atmosphere have sizes smaller than the wavelength of visible light. They scatter blue light much more intensely than red. In space where there is no atmosphere, astronauts see a pitch-black sky.

title: Module 1: Charge, Current and Potential Difference
description: Charge units, battery electromotive force, and measuring instruments.

blocks.heading: The Circuit Loop
blocks.body: Electric current flows from the positive terminal to the negative terminal of a cell (conventional direction), which is opposite to the actual motion of electrons. The potential difference maintained by chemical reactions inside the cell does work to push charges around the conducting loop.

blocks.heading: Primary Definitions
blocks.body:
I = Q / t [Amperes]
V = W / Q [Volts]

title: Module 2: Ohm's Law and Resistivity Calculations
description: Derive Ohm's law, V-I slope, and factors affecting conductor resistance.

blocks.heading: Resistance in Real Wires
blocks.body: As electrons drift through metallic lattice, they collide with oscillating metal ions, creating resistance. Thick short wires have minimal resistance, making them ideal for transmission cables.

blocks.heading: Geometry Equation
blocks.body:
R = rho * L / A
Unit of rho: Ohm * meter (Omega * m)

title: Module 1: Joule's Law of Heating & Safety Fuse
description: Heat dissipation mechanism, heating appliances, and short-circuit protection.

blocks.heading: Thermal Dissipation
blocks.body: When electrical potential drives charges through high-resistance elements (like Nichrome), collisions convert electrical energy into heat. Electric heaters, kettles, and irons exploit this to provide controlled thermal output.

title: Module 2: Electrical Power & Commercial Billing
description: Watt ratings, appliance energy calculation, and utility unit tariffs.

blocks.heading: Commercial Energy Billing
blocks.body: Utility electricity meters measure energy in kilowatt-hours (kWh). 1 kWh corresponds to the consumption of an appliance consuming 1000 Joules every second continuously for 1 hour.

title: Module 1: Field Lines & The Oersted Discovery
description: Bar magnets, compass needles, field line properties, and non-intersection proof.

blocks.heading: Magnetic Fields in Space
blocks.body: In 1820, Hans Christian Oersted noticed a compass needle deflecting when placed near a current-carrying metallic wire. This was the first empirical proof connecting electricity and magnetism into the unified force of electromagnetism.

title: Module 2: Solenoids & Electromagnets
description: Helical coils, core permeability, and creating switchable industrial magnets.

blocks.heading: Solenoid Physics
blocks.body: When current flows through multiple circular loops wound tightly into a cylinder, fields from individual turns add constructively inside the core while canceling outside. An iron rod inserted in the core becomes a powerful electromagnet.

title: Module 1: Magnetic Force & The Electric Motor
description: Lorentz magnetic force, coil torque, split rings, and commercial motor efficiency.

blocks.heading: The Motor Principle
blocks.body: When an electric current flows through a rectangular coil placed in a magnetic field, the two opposite arms experience equal and opposite perpendicular forces given by Fleming's Left-Hand Rule, setting up a continuous rotational torque.

title: Module 2: Domestic Electric Circuits & Earthing
description: Live, neutral, earth wires, fuse ratings, and short-circuit prevention.

blocks.heading: Household Safety
blocks.body: Household circuits are wired in parallel so that every appliance receives the full 220 V mains voltage and can be switched independently without disrupting other rooms. The green earth wire provides a low-resistance path straight into a copper plate buried deep in the ground.

title: Module 1: Inertia, Momentum and Newton's Second Law
description: Concept of inertia, momentum definitions, and F = ma derivations.

blocks.heading: The Origin of Force
blocks.body: Galileo realized that an object in motion does not need a continuous push to stay in motion; friction is the hidden force stopping everyday objects. Newton codified this into his first two laws.

title: Module 1: Gravitation & Free Fall Dynamics
description: Universal inverse-square law, Cavendish experiment, and calculating g.

blocks.heading: Gravity Holds the Universe Together
blocks.body: From the fall of an apple to the elliptical orbit of planets around the sun and the tidal pull of the moon, one universal law governs all celestial and terrestrial attraction.

title: Module 1: 1D Calculus Kinematics (JEE / NEET Focus)
description: Differentiate displacement polynomials, integrate variable accelerations, and analyze v-t slopes.

blocks.heading: Continuous Motion Analysis
blocks.body: In advanced competitive physics, acceleration is rarely constant. Whether analyzing air drag where a = -k*v or spring restoration where a = -omega^2*x, differentiation and integration connect position, velocity, and time seamlessly.

title: Module 1: Coulomb's Vector Law & Electric Dipoles
description: Coulomb vector form, dipole axial/equatorial fields, and dipole torque dynamics.

blocks.heading: Electrostatic Field Vectors
blocks.body: Electric field lines originate on positive charges and terminate on negative charges. They provide a geometric visualization of field intensity (line density) and direction (tangent).

title: Module 2: Gauss's Law & Symmetric Charge Distributions
description: Gaussian surfaces, flux integration, infinite wire, and conducting sheet fields.

blocks.heading: Power of Gauss's Law
blocks.body: For high-symmetry distributions (cylindrical, planar, spherical), Gauss's theorem replaces complicated Coulomb vector integrals with a single scalar equation relating flux to enclosed charge.
